  AN IRREDUCIBLE ELEMENTARY NET OVER AN ALGEBRAIC
            EXTENSION THAT IS NOT CLOSED

                                        GROUPTHEORY50


        Abstract. For every order n ≥ 3 we construct an irreducible elementary net of
        modules over a principal ideal domain in an algebraic extension of its fraction field
        that is not closed. The example is defined over Z inside the cubic field generated by a
        root of x3 − x − 1. This gives a negative answer to Kourovka Problem 19.48.




                                        1. Introduction
   Elementary nets, also called carpets, organize the allowed parameters of elementary
transvections in matrix groups. Kourovka Problem 19.48, proposed by V. A. Koibaev,
asks whether an irreducible elementary net of R-modules over an algebraic extension
of the fraction field of a principal ideal domain must be closed [1]. We give an explicit
counterexample.
   For pairwise distinct indices i, r, j, an elementary net σ = (σij ) satisfies
                                           σir σrj ⊆ σij .
It is irreducible if every off-diagonal entry is nonzero. It is closed if the elementary
subgroup E(σ) contains no transvection xij (a) with a ∈ / σij .

                                    2. The cubic example
  Let α be a root of
                                          α3 − α − 1 = 0,
put K = Q(α) and T = Z[α]. Since
                                           α−1 = α2 − 1,
the element α is a unit in T . Define additive subgroups
                                      A = Z ⊕ Zα ⊕ 2Zα2 ,
                           B = Z ⊕ 2Zα ⊕ Z(α2 − 1),              C = 2T.
Then C ⊆ A ∩ B and
                             AC ⊆ C,          BC ⊆ C,          C 2 ⊆ C.
  For n ≥ 3, set
                                     σ12 = A,         σ21 = B,
and let every other off-diagonal entry be C.
Lemma 2.1. The family σ is an irreducible elementary net.

Proof. All entries are nonzero. Along a path i → r → j with i, r, j pairwise distinct,
the two exceptional entries σ12 and σ21 cannot occur consecutively. Thus every product
required by the net condition is one of AC, BC, or C 2 , or is contained in an exceptional
target containing C. The displayed inclusions give the claim.                           □

                                    3. Failure of closure
     In the (1, 2) block write
                                 x(t) = x12 (t),    y(s) = x21 (s),
and for a unit t put
                                                                     
                                                               0   t
                            w(t) = x(t)y(−t−1 )x(t) =                .
                                                              −t−1 0
We have α, −1 ∈ A and −α−1 , 1 ∈ B. Hence
                                       w(α)w(−1) ∈ E(σ).
A direct multiplication gives
                                    w(α)w(−1) = diag(α, α−1 )
in the (1, 2) block. Conjugating x12 (1) by this diagonal matrix yields
                                          x12 (α2 ) ∈ E(σ).
However α2 ∈
           / A, because the coefficient of α2 in an element of A is even.
Theorem 3.1. For every n ≥ 3, the elementary net σ above is irreducible but not closed.
Proof. Irreducibility was established in Lemma 2.1, while x12 (α2 ) ∈ E(σ) with α2 ∈
                                                                                   / σ12
is exactly the failure of closure.                                                    □
Corollary 3.2. By Theorem 3.1, Kourovka Problem 19.48 has a negative answer, already
for the PID R = Z and the cubic algebraic extension K = Q(α).

                                         4. Perspective
   The mechanism is a rank-two diagonal element manufactured from allowed elementary
transvections. Its conjugation rescales an allowed parameter outside the prescribed
module. This provides a compact obstruction to closure that persists in every rank
n ≥ 3.

    [2] R. Steinberg, Lectures on Chevalley Groups, Yale University, 1968.
